evidence_quotes.quote: Compliance with the SDWA does not equate with safe drinking water quality, so this study cannot be considered an environmental justice analysis of access to safe drinking water.
Another potential limitation is that this analysis does not include areas served by private wells, which are more prevalent in rural areas and do not undergo routine monitoring for SDWA violations.
The type of CWS ownership (i.e., private vs. public) may have an effect on SDWA compliance and has been included in several previous studies
A negative binomial regression model was used to determine which characteristics of the water system and population served by the water system best predicted the number of violations.

Health-based violations consist of exceedances of MCLs, exceedances of disinfectant concentration thresholds, and improper water treatment (U.S. EPA, 2017c). Non-health-based violations include failure to monitor regularly or report results on-time, failure to notify the public that there is a serious health problem with drinking water, and failure to publish annual consumer confidence reports (U.S. EPA, 2017c).

criterion_notes.c1: Examines regulatory drinking-water quality and monitoring/reporting compliance (SDWA violations) among already-operating community water systems (CWSs), excluding areas served by private wells and explicitly noting it is not an analysis of access to safe drinking water or household/community service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: yes, because the study analyses compliance with a federal statute (the Safe Drinking Water Act) and includes public vs. private utility ownership as an institutional covariate. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: no, because no rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility, tenure/documentation, tariffs, disconnection/enforcement of access, or utility ownership/regulatory structure governing service access) is examined; SDWA violation counts are the dependent water-quality/monitoring variable and public vs. private ownership is tested only as a predictor of regulatory quality/monitoring violations.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical quantitative study analysing 1,694 active CWSs in Pennsylvania (2012-2016 SDWIS violation records combined with U.S. Census ACS data) using four GIS spatial estimation methods and negative binomial regression.
criterion_notes.c4: Outcomes are solely counts of total SDWA violations and health-based SDWA violations (contaminant MCL exceedances, treatment-technique violations, and monitoring, reporting, or notification failures). No outcome measuring service access, connection, service availability, continuity/reliability, quantity, affordability, or disconnection/exclusion is reported.
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (1,694 active CWSs in Pennsylvania), exposures/covariates (GIS spatial estimation method, poverty rate, percent people of color, rural/urban classification, public/private ownership, system size, water source, purchased water), outcomes (total and health-based SDWA violation counts, 2012-2016), and cross-sectional spatial regression design are clearly identified.

study_design: Observational cross-sectional spatial and statistical analysis (negative binomial regression comparing four GIS spatial estimation methods)
population_and_sample: Active community water systems (CWSs) in Pennsylvania (1,833 active CWSs in PA DEP shapefile; final analytical sample n = 1,694 CWSs across 3,166 census tracts and 67 counties)
exposure: GIS spatial estimation methods (areal weighting, dasymetric mapping, areal interpolation, county-level assignment), community sociodemographics (percent below poverty line, percent people of color, rural vs. urban), and CWS characteristics (public vs. private ownership, system size <200 connections, purchased vs. unpurchased water, groundwater vs. surface water source)
outcome: Counts of total Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) violations and health-based SDWA violations per community water system (2012-2016)
rationale: Exclude under E04 (Wrong outcome). Although this empirical GIS and negative binomial regression study examines community water systems in Pennsylvania and includes public vs. private utility ownership alongside demographic predictors, its sole outcomes are counts of total and health-based Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) regulatory violations (contaminant MCL exceedances, improper water treatment, and monitoring/reporting/notification failures) among active water systems. Per the protocol's scope discipline and Criterion 4, drinking-water quality and regulatory monitoring violation counts do not measure water service access, connection, service availability, reliability/continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion, and under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification no rule-type mechanism governing service access is analysed. (Statistical significance or direction of results played no role in this decision.)
